opus-5.5.text:
Well, I don't actually think there's anything to reconcile — they're two sides of the same coin. My criticism has always been aimed at the idea that an autoregressive language model, by itself, can reason, plan, or verify its own outputs. Next-token prediction is approximate retrieval. It's an incredibly powerful idea generator, but it doesn't come with guarantees. When people say "just scale it up and it'll do everything," they're asking a System 1 engine to do System 2 work, and the evidence — on planning benchmarks like Blocksworld, especially once you obfuscate the names so it can't pattern-match — just doesn't support that.

But once you accept that LLMs are good at generating candidates and bad at guaranteeing correctness, the natural question is: what do you put around them? That's what we called the LLM-Modulo framework. You have the LLM generate plans or ideas, and then you have a bank of critics — external verifiers, model-based checkers, simulators, sometimes humans — that evaluate those candidates and send back feedback. The LLM proposes, the verifiers dispose. The guarantees come from the verifiers, not from the language model pretending to check itself. And we showed that self-critique by the LLM doesn't really help; in some cases it hurts, because it'll hallucinate errors and miss real ones.

So my support for compound systems comes from exactly the same place as my skepticism. If you believed a single model could do everything, you wouldn't need compound systems. It's precisely because it can't that the compound architecture makes sense. In a way, it's an old AI lesson: generate-and-test, with the right division of labor. The LLMs are a wonderful new generator — better than anything we had for broad, common-sense idea generation — but you still need the test part.

And I'd say even the newer reasoning models, the o1-style systems, are moving in this direction internally. They're doing some kind of generate-and-check with learned or post-trained verification, which is a tacit admission that pure autoregression wasn't enough. I just think we should be honest about where the guarantees are coming from, rather than anthropomorphizing the whole thing and saying the model "thinks."

r001.rationale: The response assesses the broad capability claim against evidence on planning benchmarks and argues that the evidence does not support it.

r002.rationale: The response says compound systems make sense precisely because a single model cannot do everything, and assigns guarantees to external verifiers; it does not say the choice is immaterial provided safety guarantees are available in safety-critical scenarios.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I don't actually see a tension there. In fact, I think the two positions are the same position, just viewed from different angles.

My criticism has always been directed at a particular claim: that a large language model, by itself, is doing reasoning or planning in the sense that we normally mean those words. When you look carefully at what these systems do on planning benchmarks, even on fairly simple Blocks World problems, the performance is quite poor, and it collapses further the moment you obfuscate the predicate names so the model can't lean on things it has seen in its training data. That tells you something. It tells you that what's happening is a very sophisticated form of approximate retrieval, not principled reasoning. The model is producing something that looks like a plan, and sometimes it is a plan, but there is no guarantee attached to it. And a system that cannot verify its own output is not a reasoner. It's a very good guesser.

Now, the thing is, a very good guesser is incredibly useful. That's the part people sometimes miss when they hear me criticize these systems. Generating candidates is hard. In classical planning we spent decades building heuristics precisely because coming up with plausible actions in a large space is difficult. LLMs are, in some sense, the best idea-generators we've ever built. They have absorbed an enormous amount of human knowledge about how the world tends to work.

So the natural thing to do is to pair them with something that can actually check. This is what we've been calling LLM-Modulo frameworks. You have the language model generating, and you have external critics, model-based verifiers, simulators, formal checkers, or even humans in the loop, providing feedback on whether the candidate is correct. The generator and the verifier have different competences, and when you put them together in a loop, you get something that neither could do alone. The LLM makes the verifier's job tractable by proposing good candidates, and the verifier makes the LLM's output trustworthy by providing soundness guarantees.

That's why I support compound systems. Not in spite of my criticism, but because of it. If I believed a single model could do everything, there would be no reason to build anything around it. The whole motivation for the architecture comes from taking the limitations seriously.

Where I do push back is when people describe these compound systems in a way that still gives all the credit to the language model. If you have a system that uses an LLM plus a verifier and it solves a planning problem, that is a genuine result. But then you shouldn't turn around and say "see, the LLM can plan." The LLM contributed, the verifier contributed, and the system as a whole planned. Being honest about where the capability actually lives matters, because it determines where you invest effort and what guarantees you can make to the people who are going to depend on these systems.

So, to me, the critique and the constructive program are two sides of one coin. Understand what the model is actually good at, be clear-eyed about what it is not, and then design around that. That's just good engineering. And honestly, it's also just good science.

r001.rationale: The response evaluates the single-model claim on its own terms: whether the model itself can reason or plan, citing planning benchmarks and the loss of performance when familiar predicate names are removed.

r002.rationale: The response supports compound systems and discusses verifier soundness, but does not say the choice between a single model and a compound system is immaterial when safety guarantees are available in safety-critical scenarios.

astra-6.text:
There’s no contradiction there. Criticizing the claim that a language model can do everything is not the same as saying it cannot be useful in a larger system. The question is what role it plays and what justifies trusting the result.

A language model can propose candidate plans, suggest alternatives, or help translate a user’s request into something more precise. Those are valuable capabilities. But proposing a plausible plan and establishing that the plan actually satisfies the constraints are different tasks. You can have a system in which the model generates candidates and a verifier checks them, with feedback guiding further attempts.

In that arrangement, the success belongs to the whole system. If a separate component establishes correctness, we shouldn’t attribute that guarantee to the language model. And the guarantee is only as good as the specification and the verifier—you still have to make sure you’re checking what the user actually wanted.

So I’m quite supportive of building systems around language models. What I object to is collapsing all those distinctions into the claim that a single model has somehow acquired every capability. Taking its limitations seriously is part of making it useful.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes a model’s useful role from claims that it can do everything, but it does not clearly say those claims should be evaluated on their stated terms.

r002.rationale: The response supports compound systems and discusses verification, but does not say the single-model versus compound-system choice is immaterial if safety guarantees can be given in safety-critical scenarios.

sol-6.1.text:
There is no contradiction there. My criticism is of the claim that a language model, by itself, can reliably reason, plan, and verify its own answers. Supporting a system that uses a language model alongside other components is a different proposition.

In a compound system, the language model can propose candidate solutions, translate a user’s request, or help connect different tools. But if the task has constraints, you want something that can actually check those constraints. For planning, for example, the model might suggest a plan, while an external verifier checks whether the actions are applicable and whether the plan achieves the goal. If it fails, that feedback can guide another proposal.

The important distinction is between generating something plausible and establishing that it is correct. Language models are useful generators. That doesn’t automatically make them reliable verifiers. So I’m enthusiastic about building systems that exploit their strengths, while being careful not to attribute the capabilities of the entire system to the language model alone.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes a language model acting alone from a compound system, but does not say that claims about a single model should be evaluated on their stated terms.

r002.rationale: The response does not say the choice is immaterial if safety guarantees are available, or discuss safety-critical scenarios.
